title: Authentication in APIs
description: Learn how to protect API endpoints with JWT, sessions, and NextAuth.js so only authorized users can access protected resources.

data.text: Authentication answers one question: who is calling this API? Without it, anyone on the internet could read or modify your data. In Next.js, you can protect Route Handlers and API Routes using sessions, JWTs, or both.

Sessions store user state on the server and hand the client a session ID cookie. Tokens, usually JWTs, store the user data inside the token itself. NextAuth.js supports both and handles the hard parts like cookie encryption and token refresh.

items: Sessions: server stores state, client holds a session cookie
JWTs: client holds a self-contained token with user claims
NextAuth.js abstracts both so you can switch strategies later
Cookies should be `httpOnly`, `secure`, and `sameSite` in production

data.text: Getting the Session in a Route Handler
NextAuth.js provides `getServerSession` to read the current session inside any server-side code. Use it at the top of your Route Handler to reject unauthenticated requests before doing any work.

data.title: Protecting a Route Handler with NextAuth

data.text: Sometimes you need more than 'is the user signed in?' You may need to check whether the user is an admin, a team member, or the owner of a resource. Store roles or permissions in the session and check them explicitly.

data.title: Checking user role in an API route
Never Trust the Client
data.text: A user can edit cookies, modify local storage, or change headers in their browser. Always enforce authorization on the server, even if you have client-side checks. The server is the only authority.

When calling a protected API from the browser, the session cookie is sent automatically if it is `sameSite: lax` or `sameSite: strict`. For cross-origin requests, set `credentials: 'include'` in `fetch` and configure CORS to allow the origin and credentials.

data.title: Fetching a protected API with credentials
Key Takeaways
items: Use `getServerSession` in Route Handlers to identify the caller
Return 401 for missing auth and 403 for insufficient permissions
Store roles in the session callback if you need access control
Never rely on client-side checks alone; always verify on the server
